title: Teen Chess Master Md Imran Risks US Scholarship as Visa Deadline Closes In
excerpt: The 17-year-old International Master's approved F-1 visa was in the passport he lost in Bratislava. Four months without a US appointment, he must be stamped by January 19, 2027 — or lose his full UTRGV scholarship.
body:
• Md Imran, a 17-year-old International Master from Andhra Pradesh, holds a full scholarship to the University of Texas at Rio Grande Valley — but cannot take it up until a US consulate puts an F-1 visa into his replacement passport.
  • His original passport, containing his approved F-1 visa, was lost in Bratislava in June 2026. He says he has tried every day for four months without securing a US visa appointment.
  • He has already deferred admission from Fall 2026 to Spring 2027. His new orientation is January 19, 2027; if he cannot secure the visa before then, he risks losing the scholarship altogether.
  • His family — his father is a police officer, his mother a homemaker — has taken on Rs 40-50 lakh in loans over two years to fund a European playing circuit that costs Rs 1.5-3 lakh a month. No verified fundraiser for Imran was reported in the coverage.

Md Imran has done the hard part. The 17-year-old from Andhra Pradesh is an International Master with two Grandmaster norms, a peak rating of 2503, and a full scholarship to the University of Texas at Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) in Brownsville, Texas. What he does not have is a visa stamp in a valid passport — and without one by January 19, 2027, the scholarship itself is at risk, he told the Times of India.

How an approved visa was lost

Imran's F-1 student visa had already been approved and sat in his passport when, in June 2026, he lost the passport — along with his phone, money and belongings worth an estimated Rs 6-7 lakh — in Bratislava, Slovakia, during a European tournament trip. The passport also held his Schengen visa. The Indian Embassy in Budapest issued a replacement passport on June 29 and he returned to India on July 6, but a visa cannot simply move to a new passport: a replacement F-1 must be issued by a US consular post, and that requires an appointment.

That appointment has not come. "I waited in Europe and tried for a U.S. appointment all the way through August, September, and October," he said — despite trying every day for four months since the June incident, he has not secured one. He missed UTRGV's Fall 2026 orientation on August 23 and deferred his admission to Spring 2027. His Schengen position, at least, has eased: after a 14th application, the Hungarian Consulate in Mumbai granted him a one-year visa on October 24.

"My life is currently at a critical crossroads. Between the heavy financial debts of playing professional chess, the constant struggle to secure my final GM norm, and the looming threat of losing my U.S. university scholarship if I can't resolve my visa crisis by Spring 2027, the situation is completely overwhelming."

— Md Imran, to the Times of India

The arithmetic behind the chess

Imran's story, told at length to ChessBase India in June, is also about what elite junior chess costs a middle-class family. Playing professionally in Europe runs to Rs 1.5-3 lakh a month across flights, visas, accommodation, entry fees and food. His parents — his father a police officer, his mother a homemaker, based in Kakinada — have accumulated loans of around Rs 40-50 lakh over the last two years alone, and, in his words, "were even willing to put our family home up as collateral." He says he built his career without formal high-end coaching, and that requests for help to the Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister's Office and other leaders, through state sports incentive schemes, have so far gone unanswered.

On the board, the return on that sacrifice is nearly complete: two closed GM norms banked and one final open Swiss norm needed for the Grandmaster title, with a current rating of 2477. He returns to the European circuit on November 19 — Funchal in Portugal, then El Llobregat and Sunway Sitges in Spain, then the Rilton Cup in Stockholm over New Year — chasing that last norm while the visa clock runs.

What happens next

Everything now turns on a single administrative step: a US consular appointment, and a reissued F-1, before UTRGV's January 19, 2027 orientation. If he makes it, the scholarship converts years of family debt into a degree and a US collegiate chess career. If he cannot, he has said, the scholarship is lost — and one of India's most productive young players is left to fund the Grandmaster chase the way he has funded everything so far: tournament by tournament, loan by loan.
